title: Chapter 40 – The Inspector
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Cheng Yun]

Cheng Yun walks up Green Pine Hill because he has learned that a man who rides to an audit is remembered as an official, and a man who walks is remembered as a guest.

It is the third week of spring. The snow has gone from the valley floor and lingers only in the north-facing hollows, in gray crusts that crack underfoot. The road climbs through young pine and last year's bracken, and every hundred paces a stream crosses it, brown and loud with melt. He carries a leather satchel, a folding stool and a bundle of blank rolls. He has left his horse and his clerk at the foot of the hill. It is a small discourtesy to the Sect, and he will write a note to himself about it later.

He is thirty-eight, and has been a Foundation Establishment cultivator for eleven years, mid stage for the last four. It is not a great achievement, as the Sect measures such things. He knows men who reached the stage at twenty-two and are now teaching in the Inner Court. He reached it by a long, dull road, ledger by ledger, deed by deed, because he is a man who believes that the truth is a kind of weight, and that if you keep adding small true things to a scale it will eventually tip.

The gate comes in sight around the last bend: a wall of plain gray stone, a pair of oak doors, a tower with a bell. Smoke rises behind it from a chimney that leans at an angle. A stink of hot iron rides the breeze.

Seven hundred and fifty years of the Compact, he thinks. And I have never walked into a house where I was less certain what I was going to find.

He stops at the gate and gives his name to the guard. And because he has been trained to notice, he also notices the guard.

A young man, nineteen perhaps, in the gray tunic of the clan. Broad in the shoulder and slow of face, with a bronze arm-guard on his left forearm and a spear in his right hand. Qi Refining, third stage, a mortal-grade barrier ring on his belt. He stands correctly. He does not look at Cheng Yun's face. He looks at his hands.

They have been told to watch the hands, Cheng Yun thinks. A good habit. Someone has been teaching them.

"The Patriarch is expecting you, Inspector," the guard says. "I will take you to the hall."

* * *

Lin Wenyuan receives him in the study, standing, in a plain brown house robe with his left hand folded over his right.

He is not what Cheng Yun expected. The file says forty-seven. The man in front of him looks older and younger at once, with a face lined by pain and a stance as upright as a post. His eyes are tired. His hands, which Cheng Yun studies for a long moment, are the hands of a very good calligrapher: long, steady, the first two fingers of the left hand stained blue-black with ink.

"Inspector Cheng." He bows exactly as the Compact requires. "You are welcome on Green Pine Hill. I hope your son-in-law is better. Heir Feng mentioned that he had been ill."

For one moment Cheng Yun is genuinely surprised. He does not have a son-in-law. He has a married niece in the east, and a nephew with a bad lung. But Lin Feng, in the one conversation they had at the foot of the Hundred-Stair, had asked if the inspector's family was well. It had been a polite young man's question. He had answered it with a polite lie. My nephew is ill. It has traveled up a mountain and into a letter and across a valley and has been given back to him, slightly changed, by a man who remembers everything.

Careful, he thinks, with a faint private amusement. Someone is paying attention.

"My nephew is improving, thank you." He sets down his satchel. "Patriarch Lin. I will be plain. I am here for the audit that follows a change of Patriarch. I will need the tribute rolls for the last three years, the treasury, the guard's muster, the household register, and the deed. I will also need to speak with whoever keeps the accounts, and with any person who has handled the Sect's tribute. I will be on the hill three days."

"All of it is ready."

"It is?"

"My accountant, Elder Aunt Lin Wenjun, has had the books in order since the autumn. I believe she has been waiting for you with some impatience." The corner of the Patriarch's mouth moves. "I would advise you not to question her figures unless you are prepared to be corrected."

"I will bear it in mind."

"I would also like to say one thing before you begin." The tired eyes meet his. "My father's death, and my second brother's, were irregular. Some things in this house were done in haste. I will not tell you that everything was done correctly. I will tell you that nothing was done in order to deceive the Sect. If you find a gap, ask me. I will not hide it."

It is the best opening a man could have made. Cheng Yun has seen a hundred Patriarchs, and perhaps three of them said anything like it. He is aware that his sympathies, which he prides himself on keeping in a locked drawer, have shifted a little.

That is exactly the sort of thing a clever man says, he reminds himself.

"I will ask," he says. "Thank you."

* * *

Elder Aunt Lin Wenjun is sixty, gray-haired, thin as a bundle of twigs, and utterly without fear.

He sits across a table from her in the long room under the library for six hours, and by the end of the first he has stopped trying to catch her out. It is not a matter of respect. It is a matter of arithmetic. She has the ledgers laid out in four neat stacks, each volume tabbed with red cloth, each entry cross-referenced to a receipt in a second set of books. When he asks a question, she answers it before he has finished asking. When he finds a figure that does not add, she reaches across the table, turns the book around, and shows him the line where it does.

"The autumn tribute," he says. "Three hundred low stones. Paid at the Willow Ford collection, on the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month. I have the Hall's receipt."

"You have two. The second is for the forty-two stones in arrears from the previous spring."

"I see it." He turns a page. "The income from the Willow Ford shop is shown as a hundred and four stones for the autumn quarter, a hundred and eighty-one for the winter, and two hundred and twenty-six for the spring so far."

"Yes."

"That is a considerable recovery."

"It is a recovery, not a miracle." She does not blink. "There are two sources. The Mirror Guard contract with the market warden at Willow Ford, which is the Pavilion's, and public. And the new refinery in the old granary. It pays about twenty-eight stones a week."

"I have heard of it. A spoil-heap operation." He keeps his voice level. "Run by an old artisan named Hu."

"A guest elder of the clan. He was taken in as a tutor to the younger son, and he has repaid us in the only currency he has." A short, dry sound that might be a laugh. "He is a drunk, Inspector. He knows it. He does not pretend otherwise. But he has a very good eye for slag."

Cheng Yun writes this down. It is not necessary. He writes it anyway.

"The loans," he says. "A sum of two hundred and eighty stones lent by the late steward to five side-branch households. The ledger shows it as forgiven."

"By the Patriarch. On the hundredth day of mourning."

"The Compact makes no provision for forgiving an inherited debt."

"No." She sets down her brush. "It makes no provision against it, either."

A small silence. Cheng Yun looks at the thin old woman across the table, and then at the line of figures in her careful hand, and thinks of the number of clans he has audited in eleven years that would have called the debt in by the third day.

"I find," he says slowly, "that I approve of it."

"Then you are the second man in the Sect who does," Wenjun says. "The first is the Patriarch. I advised against it." She folds her hands. "I was wrong. But I intend to say so only once."

* * *

The deed is the thing he has been dreading.

He has read the Arbiter's report. He has read Shen Wuye's careful, dry, unrevealing account of the spring hearing and the missing second copy, and the miraculous discovery of a duplicate behind the founder's tablet, and the unmasking of a traitor steward. He has read it three times. And each time he has had the same quiet, persistent thought, which he has not written down anywhere.

Too tidy.

It is not a fault in the report. It is a fault in the story. Deeds do not turn up behind tablets on the eve of a hearing. They turn up in the hands of lawyers, or in the ashes of fires, or not at all. The founder of the Lin clan was a careful man, by every account. He did not hide a second copy of his deed. He kept one, and registered one, and trusted the Hall to remember.

He asks to see it in the ancestral hall, because it is cold, and quiet, and he would rather examine a thing like this with nobody watching.

The deed lies on a table of black wood under a window. It is a single large sheet of hemp paper, yellowed to the color of old ivory, folded in thirds and creased with the wear of a century and a half. The writing is in a strong, slanted, practical hand. The Land Deed of the Hill Called Green Pine, Registered by Lin Shoucheng. Below it, two seals: the square red mark of the founder, and the round blue mark of the Willow Ford county, with a faint hairline crack across the circumference.

He takes out his lens.

It is a thing the Sect gives to inspectors of the Outer Affairs Hall, a disc of ground crystal in a bronze ring, Profound grade, low tier. It has one use, and a sufficiently skilled eye can do remarkable things with it. He lowers it over the paper, and lets his sense sink through the lens into the fibers.

The hemp is old. Very old. He can feel the years in it, the long slow draining of the plant's life into the paper, a century and a half of dry air and cold. The ink is pine soot and gum, of exactly the kind that was used at the time. The seal paste has the faint greasy sparkle of cinnabar and beeswax. All of it is genuine. All of it.

He goes over it a second time, more slowly, with his breath held.

There.

It is nothing. It is less than nothing. A flaw so slight that his own sense slides past it. It is in the third fold, at the very edge of the sheet, where the paper has been creased and uncreased so many times that the fibers have begun to lift. There, for the length of a grain of rice, a few fibers do not lie as the others do. They are very slightly too regular. As if each had been placed rather than grown.

He stares at it for a long time. His mouth has gone dry.

A restoration, he thinks. A very good one. Someone has repaired the fold. He tries to imagine the hand that could do it. A master of the Sect's Paper Pavilion might manage it, with a year of work and a hundred stones' worth of materials. A Foundation cultivator. A Purple Mansion elder.

Or nobody. Or the paper has simply been handled too often, and the fibers have set in a way he has never seen before.

It is not a forgery. I cannot say it is a forgery. I can say that a very slight irregularity exists in the third fold of a hundred-and-fifty-year-old document, and that I do not know the cause.

He lowers the lens, and rubs his eyes, and stands in the cold hall for a long time without moving.

I do not know the cause. That is the whole of it. And it is the third thing on this hill that I do not know the cause of.

* * *

He finds the artisan at the granary, at noon, with a flask of wine in one hand and a hammer in the other.

It is a vast, black, smoking barn of a building, with a roof patched in three colors of thatch and doors tied back to let out the heat. Inside, a long trough of water runs the length of the floor, carrying a gray silt that glitters faintly at the edges. Two boys of fourteen or fifteen are shoveling gravel into it. A line of gray ingots lies cooling on a bed of sand. At the far end, by the anvil, an old man with one sleeve pinned across his chest is hitting a lump of iron with the patient fury of a person who regards the iron as a personal enemy.

Cheng Yun stands in the doorway and says nothing for a minute.

He has read the Registry entry. Hu. Mortal artisan, no rank. He has read the Arbiter's note, which says only that the man held a gate with a bent rod. He has read, in a thin file at the bottom of a locked drawer in the Hall's archive, a very old report from the Eastern Sea. Hu Tieshou. Artifact refiner of the Coral Gate. Believed dead. He has read, in another file, a name that makes the hair rise on his arm. The Veiled Forge.

It is the most remarkable absence of evidence he has ever encountered.

"You are the inspector," says the old man, without turning.

"I am."

"You walked up the hill."

"I did."

"Pity. I was going to make a joke about officials on horses." The hammer comes down. "Sit down. Mind the pit. Do you drink?"

"Not on duty."

"You are on duty now?"

"I am always on duty."

"Then you are a very unhappy man." The old man lifts his head at last, and turns, and Cheng Yun sees his face. It is burnt, broad, deeply lined, with a crooked nose and eyes the color of ash. They are not a drunk's eyes. They are the clearest eyes he has seen in a decade. "I am told you want to know who makes the paper."

"I am told you do."

"Then you were told right. I built the machine. A Hollander beater, my own design. A screw press I took from an oil mill. A drying frame I stole from the Patriarch's laundry." He sets down the hammer. "It is not a secret. Come and look at it. Bring your lens. I know you have one. Everyone knows an inspector's lens."

Cheng Yun lets out a breath that is almost a laugh.

He goes with him, around the back of the granary, into a long low shed where the machine stands. It is crude, ugly, patched, a great wooden trough with a roller of cedar and iron, but it works. It is clearly the thing that makes the paper. He examines it for twenty minutes. He examines the gears. He examines the pulp. He holds a sheet up to the light and turns it, and runs his lens along the grain.

It is better than anything the Paper Pavilion produces. By a margin.

"This is not your work," he says.

He says it very quietly. The old man does not move.

"It is excellent," Cheng Yun goes on. "It is an ingenious machine, very cleverly made. But I have seen what Hu Tieshou makes. In the Hall's archive there are three of his early works, a pair of braces, a spiral chisel, a cauldron hook. They are beautiful, but they are for killing. They are not for this." He lowers the sheet. "Someone told you how to build it."

"Someone told me what to try."

"Who?"

The old man looks at him for a long moment. Something moves across the broad, ruined face, and is gone.

"Inspector," he says. "May I tell you a story?"

"If it is a true one."

"It is a true story. It is also, in a sense, not. It is about an old man who lost an arm, and the reason he lost it, and the thing he swore afterward, which was that he would never again make anything for a person who did not know how to use it." The ash-gray eyes do not waver. "He has been alone for fifteen years. And one day a boy came to his door. A very small boy. With a hammer. And the boy did not ask him to make a weapon. The boy asked him what he thought of a crack in a blade."

Cheng Yun says nothing.

"I will not tell you that boy's name. I will tell you that he has never, in all the time I have known him, asked me for anything that could hurt a person who did not first try to hurt him." The old man's voice is very level. "If that is a crime, I would like to hear the clause."

It is a long silence. The shed smells of wet pulp and old wine.

"There is no clause," Cheng Yun says at last.

"No."

"The Compact has a place for a man who does not wish to be asked." He folds the sheet carefully, and tucks it into his sleeve. "I will say in my report that the paper is of excellent quality and is made by a machine of Hu's design. I will say that Hu is a mortal artisan of no rank. I will say that he drinks." He pauses. "If I am asked a direct question about the Eastern Sea, I will answer that I do not know."

"Thank you."

"Do not thank me." Cheng Yun bows, a small stiff bow, the first he has made to a mortal artisan in his life. "I am an inspector of ledgers. I do not read people. It is the only reason I have lasted so long."

* * *

He does not sleep.

They have given him a room in the guest wing, a neat clean room with a paper window and a brazier and a cot, and a small bowl of boiled eggs on the table. He eats one. He lies down. He gets up again at the second watch of the night, wraps his cloak around him, and goes out onto the wall to look at the stars.

The hill is quiet. Forty-one people, asleep, breathing. The wind is soft, with a smell of snowmelt and pine resin. Below him, at the far end of the east wall, a lantern burns in the window of the granary where the old artisan sits up with his wine.

He leans on the parapet and lets his sense go out.

It is a Foundation sense, wide and calm, a tide spreading over a shore. He feels the hill as a great dark shape, sleeping, with a faint cold thrum running through it that he has been noticing for three days and cannot account for. The vein. A dying thing, the stele says. Three parts in a hundred. It feels like a man's pulse in the last hour of a long illness.

And in the quarry, below the north terrace, something else.

It is so faint that he almost passes over it. Not a person. Not a beast. A small bright flicker at the edge of his sense, round and clean, like a pebble dropped into a still pond. It is there. And then, in the instant that he turns his attention to it, it is not. It slips sideways. It does not move away. It simply is not where it was, as though the space it occupied had folded in on itself and let it through.

He stands very still.

A seam, he thinks. It is a word from an old formation text, one he has not had occasion to use in years. Something that goes through seams.

He waits for a long time with his sense held out like a hand. The flicker does not return.

Three, he thinks. The deed, the paper, and this.

He does not write it down.

* * *

On the third day, Cheng Yun goes home by the east road, and does not take the horse.

The clerk has gone ahead with the baggage. He walks alone down a long, narrow, deserted track through the pines, with the satchel on his shoulder and the report half-composed in his head. The tribute is correct. The treasury is correct. The guard is under strength and well led. The accountant is the most competent I have met. The Patriarch is honest. He turns the sentences over like stones. The deed is genuine, with an irregularity in the third fold that I cannot explain. The paper is excellent. The refinery is a sound operation.

The younger son.

He has only met him once. He was brought into the study at the end of the second day, a small boy of ten, nearly eleven, in a plain tunic, with soot on his chin and a scab on his thumb. He bowed. He said, "Inspector." He answered every question in a clear, polite voice. He said he was slow. He said he was fond of numbers. He said he helped Old Hu with the bellows.

There was nothing wrong with him. That was what Cheng Yun kept coming back to, on the road down. A pseudo-root with five dim crystals, a second-stage cultivator by the Registry's own mirror, a quiet child who counted. There was not a single thing in the boy that was out of place.

And that is the thing I cannot explain.

Three things I do not know the cause of, and one of them is a child who is perfectly ordinary.

The track curves down into a gully. It is a wet, shadowy place, with a stream along the bottom and a clump of old beeches on the far bank. A fallen cedar lies across the path. He steps over it without thinking, and stops.

There is something on the ground.

It is nothing. A patch of ash, gray and fine, no larger than a table, scattered in two low drifts at the foot of a dead oak and half washed away by the melt. Someone has strewn leaves over it. It looks like the remains of a fire, five months old, and a careless one.

He crouches. He takes a pinch between his finger and thumb.

It is cold.

Not the cold of the air. A deep, clean, dry cold, as though the ash had been burned in the heart of a glacier. It crumbles to powder at a touch, and under his sense it carries a thin, sour, familiar trace, like iron and old salt.

Blood-oil. He knows the smell. He has smelled it before, in a cave in the south, in a ditch behind a dead boy's courtyard. A blood-bowl fire. White. The kind that burns bone to nothing.

He looks at the ground for a long time. Two drifts. One of them, he realizes, is the size of a large man. The other of a smaller.

Two bodies.

He stands up slowly, with the cold powder drifting off his fingers, and looks around the gully. The oak. The beeches. The stream. The pale scar of a trail along the east bank. He looks at the trampled leaves at the mouth of the gully, where the mold has been disturbed in a regular pattern. Six small marks in a ring. A hexagon.

Pins, he thinks. Somebody set pins here. And burned the Blood Shadow's own bodies with the Blood Shadow's own oil.

The wind stirs in the beeches.

On the far side of the valley, very faint, a bell is ringing in the village at the foot of the hill. He stands in the quiet gully with the ash on his hands and looks up the long slope toward the wall of Green Pine Hill.

He does not say anything for a long time. When at last he does, it is very softly, to nobody, in the voice of a man who has just finished adding a column and found the total larger than he feared.

"The boy who counts," he says.
